scan.summary: This is an internal emergency action plan for a 42-employee chemical manufacturing facility that describes evacuation procedures, alarm systems, employee accountability, first aid, and rescue duties in the event of fire, chemical release, medical emergency, or earthquake. The plan is the company's own policy document, not a permit or certificate issued by an agency.
scan.freshness_note: This plan was revised in February 2021 and is now over five years old. Given that the plan states it is reviewed every January and requires evacuation map updates whenever building layout changes, it should be verified whether a more recent version exists (current date is September 2026).

gaps.title: No evidence of annual review completion
gaps.description: Section 6 states 'The facilities lead reviews the plan every January' but the document shows only one revision date (February 2021). No log or memo documenting the annual reviews for 2022, 2023, 2024, 2025, or 2026 is attached or referenced.
gaps.fix: Maintain a written record of each January review, signed by the facilities lead and dated, noting whether updates were needed and what changes (if any) were made to the plan or evacuation maps.
gaps.citation: 29 CFR 1910.38(a) and Oregon OSHA 437-002-0042 require emergency action plans be in writing and kept current; annual review practice should be documented to show compliance.
gaps.quote: The facilities lead reviews the plan every January and updates the evacuation maps whenever the building layout changes.

gaps.title: Appendices A and B not provided
gaps.description: The document references Appendix A (evacuation maps) and Appendix B (floor warden and first-aid responder roster) but these critical materials are not included. The plan cannot be fully evaluated for completeness without seeing the actual evacuation maps, warden roster, and responder names.
gaps.fix: Obtain and attach the current evacuation maps (Appendix A) and the current floor warden and first-aid responder roster (Appendix B) to verify they are up to date and complete.
gaps.citation: 29 CFR 1910.38(a) requires exit routes to be identified and an evacuation plan with specific assignments of personnel; rosters must be current.
gaps.locator: Section 3 (references to Appendix A) and Section 5 (references to Appendix B)
gaps.quote: Appendix A: Evacuation maps (warehouse, laboratory, offices); Appendix B: Floor warden and first-aid responder roster (posted beside each evacuation map)

gaps.title: No written internal alert procedures for contractors and visitors
gaps.description: The plan states it 'applies to...contractors and visitors while on site' and Section 2 describes the alarm system, but does not include procedures for how contractors and visitors are notified of the plan, shown the assembly point, or briefed on evacuation procedures before beginning work.
gaps.fix: Add or clarify a section requiring contractors and visitors to receive a brief orientation to the alarm signals, evacuation route for their work area, and assembly point location before starting work, with documentation of acknowledgment.
gaps.citation: 29 CFR 1910.38(a) requires procedures for employees and other on-site personnel; best practice also requires contractors be instructed in emergency procedures under 29 CFR 1910.119 (PSM) if applicable, or OSHA 3088 guidance on contractor coordination.
gaps.quote: It applies to all 42 employees at the Portland facility, including warehouse, drivers, laboratory and office staff, and to contractors and visitors while on site.

gaps.title: No documented incident coordinator designation or backup
gaps.description: Section 4 refers to 'the incident coordinator at the assembly point' who receives reports and communicates with fire department, but does not name the incident coordinator, specify when this role is activated, or identify a backup if the primary coordinator is unavailable.
gaps.fix: Name the designated incident coordinator (or specify the title/position), identify one or more backups by name or title, and document how the role is assigned for each shift (day, evening, night) and weekends.
gaps.citation: 29 CFR 1910.38(a)(1) requires an emergency action plan to identify who is responsible for emergency response; OSHA interpretation and PSM standards require clear assignment of emergency response duties.
gaps.locator: Section 4, Accounting for employees after evacuation
gaps.quote: Any person unaccounted for is reported at once to the incident coordinator at the assembly point, who passes the information to the fire department on arrival.

gaps.title: No procedures for non-English-speaking employees
gaps.description: The plan does not address how employees who do not speak English fluently will understand the alarm signals, evacuation instructions, or briefings. For a facility handling hazardous chemicals, this is a significant gap if any portion of the 42-person workforce is non-English-speaking.
gaps.fix: If any employees are non-English-speaking, provide translated key information (at minimum: alarm meanings, evacuation routes, assembly point location) and confirm comprehension through briefing or demonstration.
gaps.citation: Oregon OSHA and OSHA require emergency procedures be communicated to all employees; Title VII and workplace safety standards generally require meaningful access to safety information for all workers.
gaps.quote: Every new employee is walked through this plan, the exit routes for their work area and the assembly point on their first day.

gaps.title: No procedure for account of off-site or remote workers
gaps.description: The plan does not clarify how to account for employees who may be off-site during an emergency (e.g., delivery drivers, field technicians, sales representatives). The accountability procedure in Section 4 assumes all personnel are at the facility.
gaps.fix: Add a note stating whether any employees regularly work off-site and, if so, describe how they are accounted for in an emergency (e.g., by a separate call-in procedure, manager check-in, etc.).
gaps.citation: 29 CFR 1910.38 and OSHA guidance require accounting for all employees; if none work remotely, clarify that; if some do, plan must address it.
gaps.locator: Section 4, Accounting for employees after evacuation
gaps.quote: At the assembly point each floor warden takes a headcount of the people from their area against the daily sign-in sheet and the visitor log, which the receptionist brings out.

gaps.title: No reference to SDS accessibility or chemical inventory
gaps.description: Section 5 states that 'the SDS for the product is brought to the responders' for a chemically-exposed employee, but does not specify where SDSs are stored, how they are indexed, or how quickly they can be retrieved during an emergency. For a chemical manufacturing facility, easy access to SDS for all on-site chemicals is critical.
gaps.fix: Clarify where SDSs are stored (e.g., online database, hardcopy binder at first-aid station), how responders access them quickly (by chemical name, CAS number, product code), and confirm backup access method if primary system is unavailable.
gaps.citation: 29 CFR 1910.1200 (Hazard Communication) requires SDSs be readily available; 29 CFR 1910.38 requires plans to address emergency medical care; 1910.119 (PSM) requires process documentation including SDSs.
gaps.quote: An employee exposed to a chemical is taken to the emergency shower and eyewash at the loading dock if it can be reached safely, or to the assembly point, and the SDS for the product is brought to the responders.

gaps.title: No description of safe shutdown procedures for in-process chemical operations
gaps.description: The plan does not address shutdown procedures for active chemical processes (blending, reactions, distillation, etc.) before evacuation. This is critical for a manufacturing facility; evacuation may create hazardous conditions if equipment or reactions are left unattended.
gaps.fix: Add a section describing which processes (if any) must be partially or fully shut down before evacuation, who is responsible for each shutdown step, and any personnel who may remain at specific posts temporarily to execute safe shutdown procedures.
gaps.citation: OSHA guidance (OSHA 3088 and 1910.38 Appendix A) notes that essential plant operations may require certain employees to remain temporarily to execute safe shutdown; 29 CFR 1910.119 (PSM) requires procedures for emergency operations.
gaps.quote: When the continuous alarm sounds, all employees stop work, secure nothing that requires more than a few seconds, and leave by the nearest marked exit.

gaps.title: No mention of utility shutdown (water, gas, electricity) during emergency
gaps.description: For a chemical facility, emergency procedures may require shutting off natural gas, electricity, or water supplies to prevent fires, explosions, or chemical reactions. The plan does not address this or identify who is authorized and trained to do so.
gaps.fix: If utility shutdown is necessary, identify the location of main shut-off points, who is trained and authorized to shut them off, and when (e.g., before evacuation for gas/electricity, but only on incident coordinator authority).
gaps.citation: OSHA 1910.119 (PSM) requires procedures for managing chemical processes during emergencies; best practice for chemical facilities includes utility shutdown procedures.
gaps.locator: Section 3, Evacuation procedures and Section 6, Training and review
gaps.quote: the facilities lead shuts down the building ventilation from the mechanical room panel.

gaps.title: No documentation of first-aid responder certification or AED readiness
gaps.description: Section 5 mentions trained first-aid responders and an AED but does not specify: (a) which certifications they hold (CPR, first aid, wilderness first aid, etc.), (b) expiration dates of certifications, (c) when the AED was last inspected or had its pads/battery checked, or (d) a schedule for recertification.
gaps.fix: Document for each first-aid responder their certifications (type and expiration date). Establish and document a schedule for annual recertification and monthly AED maintenance checks.
gaps.citation: OSHA 1910.38 and best practice require competent first-aid personnel; AED manufacturers and AHA guidelines require regular maintenance and battery/pad replacement.
gaps.locator: Section 5, Rescue and medical duties, and Section 6, Training and review
gaps.quote: First aid is given at the assembly point by the trained first-aid responders (two per shift, named on the warden roster), who bring the first-aid kit and the AED from the front office.

gaps.title: Drill documentation not described
gaps.description: Section 4 states 'Evacuation drills are held twice a year, in spring and autumn' but the plan does not require written documentation of drill results, dates, attendance, problems identified, or corrective actions taken.
gaps.fix: Add a requirement to document each drill with the date, number of participants, time to evacuate, any problems observed, and corrective actions taken. Maintain these records for review during inspections.
gaps.citation: OSHA 1910.38 requires plans be effective; 29 CFR 1910.38 Appendix A recommends periodic testing and revision; OSHA interprets this to require documentation of drills.
gaps.locator: Section 4, Accounting for employees after evacuation
gaps.quote: Evacuation drills are held twice a year, in spring and autumn.

expected_missing.title: Fire Prevention Plan
expected_missing.why: OSHA 29 CFR 1910.38(b) requires employers subject to emergency action plan rules to also maintain a written fire prevention plan, often as a separate but coordinated document.
expected_missing.basis: Similar manufacturing facilities typically hold a separate fire prevention plan covering hazardous materials storage, hot work procedures, electrical maintenance, and fire suppression equipment maintenance.

expected_missing.title: Hazardous Chemical Inventory
expected_missing.why: For a chemical manufacturing facility, a current inventory of all hazardous chemicals on-site (with quantities and SDSs) should accompany the emergency action plan.
expected_missing.basis: OSHA 1910.1200 (Hazard Communication) and 1910.119 (PSM) require chemical inventory; 1910.38 requires plan to address hazardous materials present.

expected_missing.title: Process Safety Management (PSM) Program documentation
expected_missing.why: If this facility manufactures or handles highly hazardous chemicals above threshold quantities (per 29 CFR 1910.119 Appendix A), a PSM program and associated mechanical integrity, procedures, and training documents should exist.
expected_missing.basis: A chemical-manufacturing facility is likely to fall under PSM if producing or storing chemicals like chlorine, ammonia, phosgene, or flammable liquids at or above threshold quantities.

expected_missing.title: Building layout drawings with hazard zones
expected_missing.why: Emergency action plans for facilities with hazardous materials often reference hazard zones (e.g., 'flammable storage area,' 'reactive chemistry lab') on building drawings to clarify which shelter-in-place area to use and why.
expected_missing.basis: Appendix A references evacuations maps but does not appear to include hazard-zone labeling typical of chemical facilities.

expected_missing.title: Emergency contact roster with 24/7 availability
expected_missing.why: A current emergency contact list (facilities manager, plant manager, emergency coordinator, fire department, poison control, local hospital) should be maintained separately and accessible at the assembly point.
expected_missing.basis: OSHA 1910.38 does not explicitly require this but OSHA 3088 guidance and best practice recommend it, especially for chemical facilities.

expected_missing.title: Mutual aid or mutual response agreements
expected_missing.why: If the facility has agreements with neighboring businesses or the local fire department for emergency response, these should be documented.
expected_missing.basis: Some chemical facilities establish mutual-aid arrangements with neighboring tenants or off-site emergency response teams.

expected_missing.title: Permit-required confined spaces (PRCS) procedures
expected_missing.why: If the facility has confined spaces (tanks, vessels, sumps), a Permit-Required Confined Space program (29 CFR 1910.146) must accompany the emergency action plan.
expected_missing.basis: Chemical manufacturing facilities often have reactors, storage tanks, or mixing vessels that may require confined-space entry and emergency rescue procedures.

expected_missing.title: SOP for chemical-specific emergency response
expected_missing.why: Beyond general evacuation, chemical-specific procedures (e.g., 'if acetic acid spills, do X; if peroxide spills, do Y') should be referenced in or appended to the plan.
expected_missing.basis: OSHA 1910.119 and OSHA 1910.120 (HAZWOPER) require procedures for anticipated chemical emergencies; standard practice is a cross-referenced emergency-response SOP.

expected_missing.title: Feedback mechanism from drills and incidents
expected_missing.why: A procedure for capturing lessons learned from evacuation drills and any actual incidents, with documented follow-up and plan improvements, is not described.
expected_missing.basis: OSHA 1910.38 Appendix A and best practice require plans be reviewed and revised; a formal feedback loop ensures continuous improvement.

scan.confidence_notes: Confidence is high that this is an internal emergency action plan document issued by Cascade Specialty Chemicals and that the content accurately reflects sections 1–6 as written. The plan appears to address the core OSHA 1910.38(a) requirements for general industry (evacuation policy, alarm procedures, accountability, rescue duties, training). However, confidence in completeness is lower because: (1) The appendices (evacuation maps and warden roster) are not provided, preventing verification that names, assignments, and layout are current. (2) The last revision date is February 2021, now over five years ago; the plan states annual review is conducted, but no documentation of 2022–2026 reviews is included. (3) For a chemical manufacturing facility, the plan does not explicitly reference whether it is also governed by OSHA 1910.119 (Process Safety Management) or 1910.120 (HAZWOPER/emergency response) rules, which would impose additional requirements beyond 1910.38 if applicable. CASCADE SPECIALTY CHEMICALS, LLC
EMERGENCY ACTION PLAN
Portland Facility, 4410 NW Front Avenue, Portland, Oregon 97210
Revised February 2021
1. Purpose and scope
This Emergency Action Plan describes what employees of Cascade Specialty Chemicals do when there is
a fire, chemical release, medical emergency, earthquake or other emergency at the Portland facility. It
applies to all 42 employees at the Portland facility, including warehouse, drivers, laboratory and office
staff, and to contractors and visitors while on site. The plan is kept in the front office and in the warehouse
break room, and a copy is available to any employee on request.
2. Alarm system
The building has a monitored fire alarm system with audible horns and strobe lights in the warehouse,
laboratory, loading dock and offices. The alarm is monitored 24 hours a day by Cascade Fire & Safety
under a service contract. Manual pull stations are located at each exit door. The alarm is tested on the first
Monday of each month by the facilities lead. A continuous horn means evacuate. Three short horns
repeated means shelter in place because of an outdoor hazard.
3. Evacuation procedures
When the continuous alarm sounds, all employees stop work, secure nothing that requires more than a
few seconds, and leave by the nearest marked exit. Exit routes are posted on the evacuation maps at each
exit door and in Appendix A. Warehouse staff leave by the east dock doors or the north pedestrian door.
Laboratory staff leave by the laboratory's own exterior door on the south wall. Office staff leave by the
main entrance or the west stairwell. Do not use the freight lift. Do not return for belongings.
The assembly point is the far north end of the visitor parking lot, beside the flagpole, at least 150 feet
from the building. Employees assigned as floor wardens (one per area, listed on the warden roster posted
beside each evacuation map) sweep their area, close doors behind them, and report to the assembly point.
For a chemical release outdoors or a hazard that makes leaving the building unsafe, the shelter-in-place
signal sounds. Employees move to the interior conference room or the laboratory corridor, close doors,
and the facilities lead shuts down the building ventilation from the mechanical room panel.
4. Accounting for employees after evacuation
At the assembly point each floor warden takes a headcount of the people from their area against the daily
sign-in sheet and the visitor log, which the receptionist brings out. Any person unaccounted for is reported
at once to the incident coordinator at the assembly point, who passes the information to the fire
department on arrival. No one re-enters the building until the fire department or the incident coordinator
gives the all-clear. Evacuation drills are held twice a year, in spring and autumn.
5. Rescue and medical duties
Employees do not attempt rescue inside the building. First aid is given at the assembly point by the
trained first-aid responders (two per shift, named on the warden roster), who bring the first-aid kit and the
AED from the front office. An employee exposed to a chemical is taken to the emergency shower and
eyewash at the loading dock if it can be reached safely, or to the assembly point, and the SDS for the
product is brought to the responders. Emergency medical services are called for any injury beyond minor
first aid.
6. Training and review
Every new employee is walked through this plan, the exit routes for their work area and the assembly
point on their first day. Floor wardens and first-aid responders are trained annually. The plan is reviewed
with all employees whenever it is changed and whenever an employee's responsibilities under it change.
The facilities lead reviews the plan every January and updates the evacuation maps whenever the building
layout changes.
Appendix A: Evacuation maps (warehouse, laboratory, offices)
Appendix B: Floor warden and first-aid responder roster (posted beside each evacuation map)
